passage:
I'm Tejas, I'm ten, and my brother Hrithik is sixteen. Last night he shouted at Mummy because she wouldn't let him go to the late show. He said she ruins everything and slammed his door so hard the calendar fell.
This morning, weird things happened. Hrithik got up before everyone. He swept the whole flat, even under the sofa. He washed all the dishes, folded the laundry and made Mummy's tea with cardamom, the way she likes it. He put it next to her without saying anything and went back to his room.
Mummy looked at the tea for a long time. She drank it. Then she said to me, quietly, "It's lovely tea. I'd still like to hear him say sorry."
I don't know what Hrithik is thinking. But the calendar is back on the wall.

qa.q: How did Hrithik make Mummy's tea?
qa.a: With cardamom, the way she likes it.

qa.q: Why might Hrithik clean the whole flat instead of talking to Mummy?
qa.a: He seems to feel guilty about shouting, and hard work feels like a way to make up for it without the harder step of saying sorry.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do next to finish putting things right?
qa.a: Go to Mummy and say sorry for shouting and saying she ruins everything, so the tea and cleaning come with words she can hear.

qa.q: How does Mummy see the tea and the cleaning?
qa.a: She appreciates them and reads them as guilt, but still wants to hear a real sorry from Hrithik.

grounding: A younger sibling watches a teenager who shouted at their mother clean the whole flat and make her tea without a word, while she still waits for an apology.

passage:
Friday. Tanuja screamed at her father when he said no to the school trip. "You never trust me! You're the worst!" She slammed the door.
Saturday. Tanuja woke at six. She mopped every floor, washed the scooter, ironed Papa's office shirts and made him ginger tea. She placed it on the table and walked away before he could say anything. When her friend Zeenat called, Tanuja said, "I'm busy. Being a perfect daughter."
Sunday. Papa found her polishing the steel almirah for the second time. He sat on the bed. "Beta, the house has never been cleaner," he said gently. "But I've been waiting for something else." Tanuja's hands stopped. She stared at the cloth. "I'm sorry I called you the worst," she whispered. Papa nodded. "Thank you. Now sit. Let's talk about the trip."

qa.q: What did Tanuja make Papa on Saturday?
qa.a: Ginger tea.

qa.q: What does Tanuja's remark 'Being a perfect daughter' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Guilty about the outburst and trying to make up for it through work, half aware that she was performing instead of apologising.

qa.q: What turning point on Sunday finished the repair, and why?
qa.a: Papa gently said he was waiting for something else, and Tanuja apologised; the words did what the cleaning couldn't. 🤍

qa.q: How might Papa have felt on Saturday, receiving tea from a daughter who walked away?
qa.a: Touched by the effort but still hurt, sensing her guilt yet missing the sorry he needed.

grounding: Over a weekend a teenager who yelled at her father cleans the house and makes tea in silence, until he gently asks for the apology.

passage: Vishal, come, sit by your Rajni Dadi. I saw you scrubbing the bathroom tiles at seven this morning. The whole house smells of phenyl. You shouted at your mother last night, no? Let me tell you something. When I was fifteen, in Meerut, I screamed at my Amma because she wouldn't let me cut my hair short. The next day I swept the courtyard, drew water, made rotis for everyone and cleaned the brass pots till they shone. I didn't say one word to her. I thought the pots would speak for me. That evening Amma sat by me and said, "The pots are beautiful. Now where are your words?" I cried and said sorry, and she hugged me with flour on her hands. So, beta, the tiles are very clean. Now go and find your words.

qa.q: What did young Rajni do to the brass pots?
qa.a: Cleaned them till they shone.

qa.q: Why did young Rajni think 'the pots would speak for me'?
qa.a: She felt guilty about screaming and hoped hard work would cancel it, avoiding the harder feeling of saying sorry out loud.

qa.q: What choice is Dadi encouraging Vishal to make?
qa.a: To go and apologise to Vishal's mother in words, since the clean tiles show guilt but can't replace an actual sorry.

qa.q: How might Vishal's mother feel about the scrubbed tiles?
qa.a: She may notice the effort and guess it means sorry, but like Rajni's Amma, she may still be waiting to hear the words.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at fifteen, she cleaned the whole house after screaming at her mother, and that her mother still needed to hear sorry.

passage:
The corporation tanker came only on Sundays, at six, and Lavanya usually slept through it. But the night before, she had screamed at Amma over the sleepover she wasn't allowed to go to: "You ruin everything! I hate living here!" Then she'd slammed her door.
At five-thirty she was up. She carried every bucket down three flights, stood in the tanker queue in the dark, and hauled them back up, arms burning. She swept the whole flat. She made filter coffee the way Amma liked it, extra froth, and left it by her bed. She didn't say a word.
Sarika came out, saw the full buckets lined up in the kitchen, and looked at her daughter for a long moment. "The buckets," she said. "Thank you." She held the coffee in both hands. "And last night?"
Lavanya stared at the floor, the word stuck somewhere in her throat.

qa.q: What did Lavanya scream at Amma the night before?
qa.a: "You ruin everything! I hate living here!"

qa.q: What do the buckets, the sweeping and the coffee show about how Lavanya feels?
qa.a: They show guilt about screaming at Amma 😔; working hard without words is her way of trying to undo it without facing the apology.

qa.q: What small step would finish what the buckets started?
qa.a: Saying a simple sorry for last night's words, even briefly, since Sarika's question shows the actions alone haven't closed it.

qa.q: Why might Sarika ask "And last night?" even after the buckets?
qa.a: Sarika appreciates the work, but the words still hurt, and she needs to hear Lavanya name them to feel it's truly mended.

grounding: Shows a teenager who yelled at her mother doing hard chores and making coffee in silence the next morning, while the mother still needs to hear an actual sorry.

passage:
In their Chennai flat, Keerthana, sixteen, had shouted at Appa on Friday night when he took her phone at eleven. "You treat me like a baby! I can't stand you!" Her door banged.
On Saturday she was up before anyone. She dusted Appa's messy bookshelf and sorted it by author. She repotted his drooping money plant. At lunch there was lemon rice with extra peanuts, his favourite.
"Why are you being so weird?" her brother Sahil whispered. She ignored him.
Appa ate slowly, then looked at the neat shelf and the plant. "Very nice, kanna," he said quietly. Keerthana nodded, eyes on her plate, waiting for the moment to pass.
That night he knocked on her door. "The lemon rice was lovely. But what you said yesterday is still sitting with me. Can we talk about it?"

qa.q: What did Keerthana make for lunch?
qa.a: Lemon rice with extra peanuts, Appa's favourite.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana keep her eyes on her plate while Appa praised the shelf?
qa.a: She felt guilty about shouting, and the chores were her way of making up for it without words; being noticed made her want the moment to pass.

qa.q: What is Appa's knock at night a turning point for?
qa.a: It invites Keerthana to say the actual sorry and talk about the phone rule, which the lemon rice couldn't finish on its own.

qa.q: How does Sahil see Keerthana's sudden busyness?
qa.a: Sahil just finds it weird, not knowing it is her way of making up for shouting at Appa.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who yelled at her father tidying, gardening and cooking for him in silence, while the father still needs a real conversation and apology.
